candidate_relations.reason: MRI showed acquired-appearing unilateral atrophy and encephalomalacia without cortical tubers or subependymal nodules.
The right hemisphere was markedly atrophic with ex vacuo ventricular dilatation, whereas hemimegalencephaly requires enlargement.
Early refractory seizures and cognitive decline constitute an epileptic encephalopathy phenotype, but the calvarial compensation identifies DDMS as the structural diagnosis.
Left spastic hemiparesis and developmental delay are compatible with cerebral palsy, but the label omits the characteristic unilateral cerebral atrophy and skull changes.
Focal EEG abnormalities and recurrent seizures arise from the damaged right hemisphere, but hemispheric epilepsy does not capture the DDMS anatomy.
Cystic encephalomalacia suggests a remote hemispheric insult such as childhood stroke, but the candidate omits the compensatory calvarial thickening defining DDMS.
The fronto-parieto-temporal cystic encephalomalacia may resemble porencephaly, but no CSF-lined congenital cavity was specifically demonstrated.
Delayed motor and cognitive milestones are consequences of the early right hemispheric injury, not its syndromic diagnosis.
Recurrent seizures, fixed hemiparesis, and a diagnostic constellation of hemiatrophy plus calvarial thickening preclude no diagnosis.
A remote hemispheric stroke could account for encephalomalacia and contralateral weakness, but it does not state the resulting Dyke-Davidoff-Masson syndrome.
The long-standing nonprogressive structural injury is a static encephalopathy, yet this umbrella term omits unilateral atrophy and compensatory skull remodeling.
The imaging suggests an early-life insult, but the record reports no perinatal complication and does not date the remote right hemispheric injury.

candidate_relations.reason: Right cerebral hemiatrophy, ex vacuo ventricular enlargement, ipsilateral calvarial thickening, seizures, and contralateral hemiparesis are diagnostic of Dyke-Davidoff-Masson syndrome.
No café-au-lait lesions, optic pathway tumor, or NF1-associated imaging features accompany the unilateral cerebral injury.
Focal seizures are well supported by EEG and clinical history but represent one manifestation of the hemispheric atrophy syndrome.
There is no facial capillary malformation, leptomeningeal angioma, or tram-track calcification suggesting Sturge-Weber syndrome.
Marked hemispheric asymmetry is a brain structural abnormality, but the imaging indicates acquired atrophy with compensatory skull changes rather than an unspecified malformation.
Cystic encephalomalacia and surrounding gliosis are present in the right hemisphere, but they do not alone include the complete DDMS constellation.
Rasmussen encephalitis can produce hemiatrophy and seizures, but no progressive unilateral inflammatory MRI changes or inflammatory testing are reported.
The compensatory calvarial thickening and hyperpneumatization indicate a longstanding early insult rather than the documented course of Rasmussen encephalitis.
